references.title: Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift: Delayed Price Response or Risk Premium?
references.read_scope: Bibliographic record only; full text not obtained. Do not import exact trading rules from this source.
references.role: Historical motivation, not an executable replication specification.

references.title: Evidence that stock prices do not fully reflect the implications of current earnings for future earnings
references.read_scope: Repository metadata and indexed abstract; attempted PDF returned HTML, not the article.
references.role: Historical evidence concerning delayed response; not proof of present-day profitability.

references.title: Comparing the Post–Earnings Announcement Drift for Surprises Calculated from Analyst and Time Series Forecasts
references.read_scope: Indexed publisher abstract; full methods not read.
references.finding: Analyst-based and time-series-based surprises yield different drift estimates.
references.implication: Replacing missing consensus with year-over-year EPS is a different hypothesis, not an interchangeable data repair.

references.title: Liquidity and the Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
references.read_scope: Publisher abstract; not a full-text replication.
references.finding: Drift concentrates in illiquid stocks; estimated transaction costs consume 70–100% of the studied long-short paper profits.
references.implication: A high-beta extension must separately test liquidity, costs and market impact; paper spreads are not retail long-only returns.

references.title: Rest in Peace Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
references.read_scope: Downloaded 46-page CFR draft: introduction; sections 2.1–2.2; start of 3.1.2; sections 4 and 6. Publication metadata verified separately.
references.finding: Samples end in 2019. Analyst-surprise drift is absent in all-but-microcap stocks since 2006 and microcaps since 2016 in this study.
references.implication: Strong adverse prior, not proof about every high-beta subset in 2025. Separate eras, microcaps and surprise definitions.

references.title: News Diffusion in Social Networks and Stock Market Reactions
references.read_scope: Published abstract and metadata; February 2024 NBER revision sections 2 and 3.1. Published full-text version not independently read.
references.finding: Greater social connectedness is associated with stronger immediate reaction and weaker later drift. The read working version uses seasonal time-series SUE and 1996–2017 data.
references.implication: Positive conditional drift evidence deserves inclusion. It does not directly validate a current analyst-beat high-beta long-only strategy.

references.title: The co-pricing factor zoo
references.read_scope: Published PDF: abstract/introduction; PEAD discussion and footnote 26; Appendix A.1 factor-source entry.
references.finding: PEAD-related factors remain important in the joint stock/bond pricing exercise; the paper acknowledges reduced recent time-series predictability.
references.implication: Priced-factor evidence is a different test from profitable delayed entry after positive consensus surprises. The reported combined-SDF Sharpe must not be assigned to PEAD alone.

references.title: Keeping It Simple: How Post-earnings Return Drift Can Exist and Not Exist Simultaneously
references.read_scope: Primary HTML article, especially sections 2–3 and Table 1. No independent replication run here.
references.finding: For the reconstructed announcement-return factor over February 2001–December 2024, excluding microcaps reduces the reported t-statistic from 2.18 to 1.43.
references.implication: Examine universe and signal definitions before using significance claims. Nonsignificance is not proof of zero effect.
references.version_caveat: This critique discusses earlier paper versions. DJM final publication appeared later in 2026; do not assume every criticism applies unchanged.
